summary: Defines a protocol for an HTTP- and JSON-based security token service by specifying how to request and obtain tokens from OAuth 2.0 authorization servers. It supports impersonation and delegation, letting one token be traded for another.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like handing a ticket to a desk and getting a different ticket back that works at another door, maybe one that says you are acting for someone else.

questions: what is the act claim in a jwt
subtitle: How a client trades one security token for another, optionally to act on someone else's behalf.

tldr.problem: Plain OAuth 2.0 swaps an authorization for an access token, which is too constrained when a service needs a different token to call a backend, or needs to act for a user.
tldr.mechanism: A client POSTs to the token endpoint with a new grant type, a subject token and optional actor token, resource, audience and scope. The authorization server answers with a normal OAuth JSON response carrying the new token.
tldr.outcome: It lets an authorization server act as a Security Token Service supporting both impersonation and delegation, with JWT claims such as act and may_act to express them.

today: RFC 8693 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2020. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Exchange Tokens
sections.content:
A security token carries identity and security information across systems; JWTs and SAML 2.0 assertions are examples. A Security Token Service (STS) validates tokens it is given and issues new ones. Web services have used WS-Trust (XML and SOAP) for this, while OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) and bearer tokens (RFC 6750) became popular for authorizing access to HTTP and RESTful resources. The usual OAuth exchange is somewhat too constrained to serve as a general token exchange.

This specification extends OAuth 2.0 so that clients can ask authorization servers acting as an STS for tokens, needing only an HTTP client and a JSON parser. The requester can be a resource server: it might trade the access token it received for a more narrowly scoped one, or an entirely different kind of token, to call a backend service.

The scope is a basic request-and-response protocol. The syntax, semantics and trust model of the tokens themselves are explicitly out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the ticket you hold does not work at the next door. This RFC defines a polite way to ask the ticket desk for a new one that does.

sections.title: Delegation versus Impersonation
sections.content:
Suppose resource server A calls backend service C on behalf of user B. With impersonation, A is given B's rights in some context and is indistinguishable from B there. With delegation, A keeps its own identity and it is understood that A acts as an agent for B, who delegated some rights.

Delegation is typically shown by a composite token holding information about both the subject and the actor. In the request, the subject_token identifies the party on whose behalf the request is made and the actor_token identifies the party to whom the rights are delegated. Whether a composite token is issued is up to the authorization server and its policy.

The RFC notes that neither concept applies when a principal acts directly on its own behalf.
sections.plainLanguage: Impersonation is wearing a costume so well that everyone thinks you are your friend. Delegation is showing a note that says you are doing a job for your friend.

sections.title: The Token Exchange Request
sections.content:
The client sends an HTTP POST to the token endpoint with application/x-www-form-urlencoded parameters and normal OAuth client authentication. Omitting client authentication would let anyone holding a compromised token turn it into other tokens, so authentication supports extra authorization checks by the STS.

  • grant_type: REQUIRED, the value urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange.
  • subject_token and subject_token_type: both REQUIRED. The token for the party being represented, and its type.
  • actor_token: OPTIONAL. actor_token_type is REQUIRED when it is present and MUST NOT be included otherwise.
  • resource: OPTIONAL, an absolute URI of the target service, with no fragment. May repeat.
  • audience: OPTIONAL, a logical name for the target service. May repeat.
  • scope: OPTIONAL, space-delimited scope strings.
  • requested_token_type: OPTIONAL. If it is left out, the type issued is the server's choice.

The requested access is effectively the Cartesian product of all scopes at all target services, so clients should not ask for too many targets. The exchange is a one-time event: it does not by itself affect the validity of the input tokens and does not tightly link input and output tokens.
sections.plainLanguage: You fill in a form: here is my ticket, here is where I want to use the new one, and here is what I need it to allow. Some boxes are required and some are optional.

sections.title: Responses and Errors
sections.content:
On success the authorization server returns HTTP 200 with a JSON body, as in normal OAuth. access_token (the issued token, even if it is not really an OAuth access token), issued_token_type and token_type are REQUIRED. expires_in is RECOMMENDED. scope is REQUIRED if it differs from the requested scope. A refresh_token is OPTIONAL and typically not issued when one temporary credential is traded for another.

token_type says how to use the token, such as Bearer. If the issued token is not usable as an access token, the value N_A is used. This is a different thing from issued_token_type, which says how the token is represented.

If the request is invalid, or a subject or actor token is invalid or unacceptable by policy, the server MUST return the invalid_request error. If it will not or cannot issue a token for a requested target, it SHOULD use invalid_target.
sections.plainLanguage: If the desk says yes, you get the new ticket and a note about how long it lasts. If it says no, you get a note saying whether your form was wrong or the door you named is not allowed.

sections.title: Token Type Identifiers
sections.content:
The type parameters take URIs. For tokens from other parties, the URI tells the server the syntax (such as JWT or SAML 2.0) so it can parse it. For the server's own tokens, it says what the token was issued for. Other URIs MAY be used for other token types.

The RFC draws a subtle distinction. An access token is a delegated authorization decision and may or may not be formatted as a JWT; the access_token identifier means a typical OAuth access token from that server, opaque to the client. The jwt identifier says specifically that a JWT is being requested or sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Each ticket has a label that says what kind it is, so the desk knows how to read it.

sections.title: JWT Claims for Actors
sections.content:
Section 4 defines claims for JWTs and for token introspection responses. The act claim is a JSON object identifying the current actor to whom authority has been delegated. Claims such as exp, nbf and aud are not meaningful inside it. A chain of delegation is shown by nesting act claims: the outermost is the current actor and nested ones are prior actors.

A token consumer MUST consider only the token's top-level claims and the current actor when applying access control. Prior actors are informational only.

The may_act claim states that one party is authorized to become the actor for another, so the server can check whether a requested delegation or impersonation is allowed. The scope claim is a space-separated list of scopes, and client_id carries the identifier of the client that requested the token.
sections.plainLanguage: A delegation token can have a sticker saying who is acting right now. Older stickers underneath show who passed it along, but only the top one counts.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Much of the guidance in Section 10 of RFC 6749 applies, as do the security issues discussed in the JWT specification. Delegation and impersonation add their own risk: whenever one principal is given another's rights there is a potential for abuse. The RFC suggests using the scope claim, along with a limited token lifetime, to restrict where delegated rights can be used.

For privacy, tokens may contain sensitive information and MUST only be sent over encrypted channels such as TLS. When information must be kept from the client, the token MUST be encrypted to its intended recipient. Deployments SHOULD include only the minimum data needed in issued tokens.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting someone act for you can be misused, so give them a short-lived note that covers only what they need, and pass it only in sealed envelopes.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the token-exchange grant type URN and the token type URIs for access token, refresh token, ID token, SAML 1.1 and SAML 2.0 in the OAuth URI registry. It also registered the new request parameters (audience, requested_token_type, subject_token, subject_token_type, actor_token, actor_token_type) and the response parameter issued_token_type, the N_A access token type, and the JWT claims act, scope, client_id and may_act, along with the matching token introspection response parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The names used in this protocol were written in an official list so nobody else uses them for something different.
